summary: Creates an IANA registry for SIP and SIPS URI parameters and their values, and lists the existing parameters as the initial entries.

plainLanguage.summary: It starts an official list of the extra bits that can be added to SIP addresses, so everyone uses them the same way.

questions: how to register a sip uri parameter
what is the sip transport parameter
subtitle: Creates the IANA registry that keeps SIP and SIPS URI parameters from colliding.

tldr.problem: RFC 3261 lets new SIP and SIPS URI parameters and parameter values be defined, but it did not create an IANA registry to record them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC creates a sub-registry under the SIP Parameters registry, seeds it with seven existing parameters, and requires new entries to be defined in a standards-track RFC.
tldr.outcome: SIP and SIPS URI parameters become reserved words recorded in one place. The RFC is itself updated by RFC 5727.

today: RFC 3969 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 99) and is updated by RFC 5727. It updates RFC 3427.

sections.title: The Missing Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3261 allows new SIP URI and SIPS URI parameters, and new parameter values, to be defined. It omitted an IANA registry for them, and RFC 3969 creates it.

The document is a Best Current Practice and it updates RFC 3427, which documents the process for extending SIP. The update specifies how to define and register new SIP and SIPS URI parameters and their values.
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP rulebook said you may invent new address add-ons, but forgot to say where to write them down. This RFC adds the missing list.

sections.title: Who Can Register a Parameter
sections.content:
SIP and SIPS URI parameters, and values for them, MUST be documented in a standards-track RFC to be registered by IANA. That documentation MUST fully explain the syntax, intended usage and semantics of the parameter. The aim is interoperability between independent implementations and no accidental namespace collisions between dissimilar features.

Unlike other protocol registries, this one has no vendor-extension tree. It only deals with parameters and values defined in RFCs. The reason given is the concerns in RFC 3427 about extensions that may damage security, greatly increase protocol complexity, or both.

RFCs that define SIP or SIPS URI parameters, or values, MUST register them with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a name to the list you must first write a proper standard explaining exactly what it does. No sneaking in your own private names.

sections.title: Reserved Words and Unregistered Parameters
sections.content:
Registered parameters and their values are to be considered reserved words. To preserve interoperability, they MUST be used consistently with the RFC that defines them, and implementations MUST NOT use "private" or "locally defined" URI parameters that conflict with registered ones.

Unregistered parameters may still be used in implementations, but the RFC calls that risky. New parameters and values can be registered at any time, and nothing assures that they will not conflict with unregistered ones already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a name is on the list it belongs to its official meaning. You may use a made-up name that is not listed, but someone may take it later and your thing could break.

sections.title: The Sub-Registry and Its Initial Entries
sections.content:
RFC 3261 section 27 already creates IANA registries for method names, header field names, warning codes, status codes and option tags. This RFC adds a new sub-registry under the SIP Parameters registry, called SIP/SIPS URI Parameters.

Each registration MUST give the name of the parameter, whether it only accepts a set of predefined values, and a reference to the RFC defining the parameter plus any RFC defining new values for it. Because registering every value of every parameter would need many sub-registries, values are registered by reference: references to RFCs defining values appear in double brackets in the registry.

Every parameter is registered both as a SIP and as a SIPS URI parameter, even if it applies to only one scheme. That avoids two parameters with the same name but different semantics. The initial table has seven entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line on the list says the name, whether the choices are fixed, and which standard explains it. Fixed-choice names point to the standards that add choices.

sections.title: Registration Policy
sections.content: Using the terminology of RFC 2434, the registration policy is Specification Required. For this registry, the parameter MUST be defined by a standards-track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule for getting on the list is: show a written standard first. Then you can be added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The registry itself has no security considerations. As RFC 3427 notes, though, an important reason for the IETF to manage SIP extensions is to ensure that all extensions and parameters can be used securely. The supporting RFCs for parameter registrations MUST therefore give detailed security considerations for their parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is harmless on its own. But each standard that adds a name must explain how to use it safely.
